Bail petitioner, namely Umesh Kumar, who is behind the bars since 29.12.2023, has approached this Court in the instant proceedings filed under S.439 Cr.P.C, for grant of regular bail in FIR No. 142 of 2023, dated 28.12.2023, under Section 376 of IPC and Section 6 of the POCSO Act, registered at Police Station Parwanoo, District Solan, Himachal Pradesh.

sentences.text: 2. Pursuant to the notices issued in the instant proceedings, respondent-State has filed status report as well as reply.
Whether reporters of the local papers may be allowed to see the judgment?

3. In terms of order dated 22.05.2024, respondent No.2(complainant) has also filed reply, wherein prayer made on .
behalf of the petitioner for grant of regular bail has been seriously objected to.
4.

Close scrutiny of the status report as well as reply filed by the respondent-State reveals that on 28.12.2023, complainant (hereinafter referred as the "victim/ prosecutrix") (name withheld to protect his identity) aged 19 years, lodged a complaint at police Station, Parwanoo, District Solan,
Himachal Pradesh, alleging therein that she knows bail petitioner for more than 7-8 years.

She alleged that though she and bail petitioner belong to different caste, but yet were friends and during the last 7-8 years, petitioner kept on sexually assaulting her against her wishes on the pretext of marriage.

She alleged that though repeatedly bail petitioner assured her that he would solemnize marriage with her, but recently she has come to know that bail petitioner is getting marriage to some other person in February, 2024.
She alleged that lastly on 29.12.2023, bail petitioner subjected her to forcible sexual intercourse on the pretext of marriage and at present, she is pregnant.
In the aforesaid background, police lodged the FIR, as detailed hereinabove, against the petitioner on 28.12.2023 and since 29.12.2023 he is behind the bars.

5. To ascertain the factum with regard to pregnancy, if any, of the victim/ prosecutrix, police got her medically examined, .
but there is no record available in that regard.

In her statement recorded under Section 164 Cr.P.C,
victim/ prosecutrix again reiterated that bail petitioner had been sexually assaulting her against her wishes on the pretext of marriage.

Since challan stands filed in the competent Court of law and nothing remains to be recovered from the bail petitioner, he has approached this Court in the instant proceedings for grant of regular bail.

6. While fairly admitting factum with regard to filing of the challan in the competent Court of law,
Mr. B.C.Verma, learned Additional Advocate General, submits that though nothing remains to be recovered from the bail petitioner, but keeping in view the gravity of offence alleged to have been committed by him, he does not deserve any leniency.

Learned Additional Advocate General further states that there is overwhelming evidence adduced on record suggestive of the fact that prior to Umesh Kumar vs State Of Himachal Pradesh on 13 June, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/172356517/
2 24.12.2023 petitioner had sexually assaulted the victim/prosecutrix against her wishes on so many occasions.

entities.text: Umesh Kumar vs State Of Himachal Pradesh on 13 June, 2024 Indian Kanoon
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: He further submits that since prior to alleged incident on 24.12.2023, victim/prosecutrix was minor, no illegality can be said to have been committed by the Investigating Agency by invoking Section 6 of the POCSO Act.

Learned Additional Advocate General submits that though victim/prosecutrix has repeatedly stated that she was sexually assaulted by bail petitioner on the pretext of marriage, but consent, if any, of her prior to last .
incident happened on 24.12.2023 is of no consequence because at that relevant time, she was minor.

Learned Additional Advocate General states that since statement of the victim/prosecutrix is yet to be recorded, it may not be in the interest of justice to enlarge the bail petitioner on bail because in the event of his being enlarged on bail, he may not only flee from justice, but may also cause harm to the victim/prosecutrix.

7. Mr. Jeevesh Sharma and Ms. Anita, learned Legal Aid counsel appointed on behalf of the victim/prosecutrix, while opposing prayer made on behalf of the bail petitioner for grant of bail,
submit that there was no consent, if any, of the victim/ prosecutrix, rather she was repeatedly sexually assaulted against her wishes on the pretext of marriage.
Above named counsel further state that on account of sexual assault, she became pregnant on number of occasions, but was persuaded by bail petitioner to abort the pregnancy.

They further state that taking undue advantage of minority and social status of the victim/ prosecutrix, bail petitioner sexually assaulted her against her wishes and as such, he needs to be dealt with in accordance with law.
8. Having heard learned counsel for the parties and perused the material available on record, this Court finds that as .
per the statement of the victim/prosecutrix, she had a prior acquaintance with the petitioner for last 7-8 years, meaning thereby victim/prosecutrix had come in the contact of the bail petitioner somewhere in the year, 2015 and since then they had been meeting frequently.

As per own case of the victim/ prosecutrix, she and bail petitioner had maintained physical relations on so many occasions, but interestingly, there is nothing on record suggestive of the fact that complaint, if any,
was ever made by the victim/prosecutrix against the bail petitioner.

Material available on record clearly reveals that victim/prosecutrix, who is 19 years old, had been joining the company of the bail petitioner of her own volition and without there being any external pressure.

As per own statement of the victim/prosecutrix, she was being subjected to sexual intercourse by the bail petitioner on the pretext of marriage and as such, this Court finds it difficult to agree with Mr. Jeevesh Sharma and Ms. Anita, Legal Aid Counsel that repeatedly victim/prosecutrix was subjected to forcible sexual intercourse.
There is nothing on record that complaint, if any, was ever made by the victim/prosecutrix against the bail petitioner, who allegedly repeatedly persuaded her to abort her pregnancy.

For the first time, complaint with regard to sexual assault came to be lodged at the behest of the victim/prosecutrix qua the incident of 24.12.2023, by which time, victim/prosecutrix had become major.

.

sentences.text: If the statement of the victim/prosecutrix given to the police under Section 154 Cr.P.C., is read in its entirety, it clearly suggests that though she had come to know with regard to proposal of the marriage of the petitioner with some other person on 24.12.2023, but yet she again joined the company of the bail petitioner on the afore date and thereafter, she was allegedly sexually assaulted against her wishes. Since, no report with regard to incident, if any, happened prior to 24.12.2023 was ever lodged during which period, victim/prosecutrix was minor, this Court finds it difficult to agree with Mr. B.C.Verma, learned Additional Advocate General that bail petitioner sexually assaulted the victim/prosecutrix against her wishes, while she was minor.

10. Leaving everything aside, this Court after having noticed conduct of the victim/prosecutrix,
which is apparent from the record, finds it difficult to agree with the contention of learned Additional Advocate General and learned Legal Aid Counsel representing the victim/prosecutrix that she was unable to understand the consequences of her being in the company of the bail petitioner, rather material available on record, clearly reveals that victim/prosecutirx of her own volition and without there being any external pressure had been joining the company of the bail petitioner.

Though, aforesaid aspects of the matter are to be considered and decided by learned court below in totality of facts and evidence collected on record by the prosecution, but having taken note of aforesaid glaring aspects of the matter, this Court sees no reason to let bail petitioner incarcerate in jail for indefinite period during the trial, especially when his guilt, if any, is yet to be established on record by the prosecution by leading cogent and convincing evidence.

Apprehension expressed by learned Additional Advocate General that in the event of bail petitioner being enlarged on bail, he may flee from justice or may again indulge in such offences again, can be best met by putting bail petitioner to stringent conditions.

12. Hon'ble Apex Court as well as this Court have held in catena of cases that one is deemed to be innocent till the time his /her guilt is not proved, in accordance with law and as such, this Court sees no reason to curtail the freedom of the bail petitioner for indefinite period during the trial, especially when his/her guilt is yet to be proved.
It has further held by the Hon'ble Apex Court in the aforesaid judgment that a person is believed to be innocent until found guilty.

13. Recently, the Hon'ble Apex Court in Criminal Appeal No. 227/2018, Dataram Singh vs. State of Uttar Pradesh & Anr., .
decided on 6.2.2018, has categorically held that a fundamental postulate of criminal jurisprudence is the presumption of innocence, meaning thereby that a person is believed to be innocent until found guilty. Hon'ble Apex Court further held that while considering prayer for grant of bail, it is important to ascertain whether the accused was participating in the investigations to the satisfaction of the investigating officer and was not absconding or not appearing when required by the investigating officer.

The relevant paras of the aforesaid judgment are reproduced as under:
2.
A fundamental postulate of criminal jurisprudence is the presumption of innocence, meaning thereby that a person is believed to be innocent until found guilty.

However, there are instances in our criminal law where a reverse onus has been placed on an accused with regard to some specific offences but that is another matter and does not detract from the fundamental postulate in respect of other offences.

Yet another important facet of our criminal jurisprudence is that the grant of bail is the general rule and putting a person in jail or in a prison or in a correction home (whichever expression one may wish to use) is an exception.

Unfortunately,
some of these basic principles appear to have been lost sight of with the result that more and more persons are being incarcerated and for longer periods.
This does not do any good to our criminal jurisprudence or to our society.

3. There is no doubt that the grant or denial of bail is entirely the discretion of the judge considering a case but even so, the exercise of judicial discretion has been circumscribed by a large number of decisions .
rendered by this Court and by every High Court in the country.
Yet, occasionally there is a necessity to introspect whether denying bail to an accused person is the right thing to do on the facts and in the circumstances of a case.

4. While so introspecting, among the factors that need to be considered is whether the accused was arrested during investigations when that person perhaps has the best opportunity to tamper with the evidence or influence witnesses.

If the investigating officer does not find it necessary to arrest an accused person during investigations, a strong case should be made out for placing that person in judicial custody after a charge sheet is filed.

Similarly, it is important to ascertain whether the accused was participating in the investigations to the satisfaction of the investigating r officer and was not absconding or not appearing when required by the investigating officer.

Surely, if an accused is not hiding from the investigating officer or is hiding due to some genuine and expressed fear of being victimised, it would be a factor that a judge would need to consider in an appropriate case.

It is also necessary for the judge to consider whether the accused is a first-time offender or has been accused of other offences and if so, the nature of such offences and his or her general conduct.

The poverty or the deemed indigent status of an accused is also an extremely important factor and even Parliament has taken notice of it by incorporating an Explanation to Section 436 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973.
An equally soft approach to incarceration has been taken by Parliament by inserting Section 436A in the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973.
5. To put it shortly, a humane attitude is required to be adopted by a judge, while dealing with an application for remanding a suspect or an accused person to police custody or judicial custody.

There are several reasons for this including maintaining the dignity of an accused person, howsoever poor that person might be, the requirements of Article 21 of the Constitution and the fact that there Umesh Kumar vs State Of Himachal Pradesh on 13 June, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/172356517/
5 is enormous overcrowding in prisons, leading to social and other problems as noticed by this Court in In Re-Inhuman Conditions in 1382 Prisons 14.

Hon'ble Apex Court in Sanjay Chandra versus Central Bureau of Investigation (2012)1 Supreme Court Cases 49 has held that gravity alone cannot be a decisive ground to deny bail, rather competing factors are required to be balanced by the .
court while exercising its discretion.

sentences.text: It has been repeatedly held by the Hon'ble Apex Court that object of bail is to secure the appearance of the accused person at his trial by reasonable amount of bail.
The object of bail is neither punitive nor preventative.

15. In Manoranjana Sinh alias Gupta versus CBI, (2017) 5 SCC 218, Hon'ble Apex Court has held that the object of the bail is to secure the attendance of the accused in the trial and the proper test to be applied in the solution of the question whether bail should be granted or refused is whether it is probable that the party will appear to take his trial.

entities.text: Manoranjana Sinh alias Gupta versus CBI, (2017) 5 SCC 218
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: Otherwise also, normal rule is of bail and not jail.

Apart from above, Court has to keep in mind nature of accusations, nature of evidence in support thereof, severity of the punishment, which conviction will entail, character of the accused,
circumstances which are peculiar to the accused involved in that crime.

16. The Apex Court in Prasanta Kumar Sarkar versus Ashis Chatterjee and another (2010) 14 SCC 496, has laid down various principles to be kept in mind, while deciding petition for bail viz. prima facie case, nature and gravity of accusation, punishment involved, apprehension of repetition of offence and witnesses being influenced.

sentences.text: In view of above, bail petitioner has carved out a case for himself.
Consequently, present petition is allowed.
